Chelonia mydas exhibits incipient life stages characterized by a precise metabolic endowment that sets the energetic boundaries for early development. The initial energy content of the egg has been measured at 226,000 Joules , a substantial yolk investment that supports embryogenesis entirely prior to any exogenous intake. Under controlled incubation conditions at a mean temperature of 30.22 °C [T = 30.22 °C], the embryonic period culminates in hatching at 47.69 days , and the broader interval to the onset of exogenous feeding—including emergence from the nest and the initial swim frenzy—spans approximately 54 days [ab = approximately 54 days]. These thermal requirements are critical, as small deviations in nest temperature can significantly alter the duration of embryogenesis. At the moment of hatching, neonates display a straight carapace length of 4.55 centimeters , a dimension that remains essentially unchanged through the first days post-emergence until feeding commences. The average wet weight of a Ningaloo hatchling, inclusive of residual yolk, is 27.02 grams , reflecting the dense yolk reserves that must sustain the animal through its energetically demanding dispersal phase.

The juvenile and sub-adult phases of Chelonia mydas are marked by a gradual but extensive increase in body dimensions, culminating in the massive sizes observed in adult populations at Ningaloo. Field surveys conducted by CSIRO at this important rookery indicate that the ultimate curved carapace length of the largest individuals approaches 115 centimeters [Li = 115 centimeters], a value that aligns with the typical maximum for the region. However, the largest published record of curved carapace length for the species globally stands at 143 centimeters [Li = 143 centimeters], representing an exceptional individual. Concomitant with this impressive skeletal growth, the ultimate wet weight recorded during CSIRO field trips for the heaviest turtle encountered was 130,000 grams [Wwi = 130,000 grams], a mass that underscores the substantial energy reserves an adult must accumulate. A sexually mature female must reach a minimum threshold before she can invest in reproduction; at Ningaloo, the smallest nesting female encountered displayed a curved carapace length at puberty of 91 centimeters [Lp = 91 centimeters], and her wet weight at puberty was 97,000 grams [Wwp = 97,000 grams]. These morphological benchmarks provide crucial reference points for population monitoring and conservation status assessments of this long-lived species.

Reproductive output in the green turtle is constrained by a life-history strategy that balances high fecundity per event with a low frequency of breeding years. Field studies at Ningaloo have documented that a single sexually mature female produces an average of 105 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 105 eggs per clutch], laying this clutch approximately four times within a single nesting season [F_R_i = approximately four times within a single nesting season]. However, after this intense annual effort, the same female typically does not return to nest for another three years, resulting in a nesting interval of roughly four years between successive breeding seasons. When these values are integrated over her lifetime at a mean environmental temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate is realized through the combination of these clutch and frequency parameters. This asynchronous reproductive schedule is an adaptation to the extreme energetic demands of egg production and the long migrations between foraging grounds and nesting beaches, which together impose a significant physiological cost that necessitates prolonged recovery periods between reproductive bouts.

The temporal dimension of the green turtle's life cycle is remarkable, with individuals exhibiting one of the longest lifespans among marine reptiles. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations at Ningaloo have been estimated to achieve a lifespan of approximately 80 years [am = approximately 80 years], a longevity that requires decades of somatic growth and maintenance before reproduction can commence at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Correspondingly, the time elapsed since birth to the first successful reproductive event is substantial; analysis of mark-recapture data from CSIRO field trips indicates that this milestone is reached at around 29 years since birth [tR = around 29 years since birth] when the turtles are living under thermal conditions averaging 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive period is a defining feature of the species' slow life-history strategy, allowing individuals to accumulate the immense body mass needed to support the high energetic costs of long-distance migrations and repeated reproductive episodes. In contrast, the brief, temperature-sensitive incubation period that gives rise to these long-lived individuals highlights the profound contrast between early-life vulnerability and adult resilience in this species.

Comparative physiological studies reveal that the green turtle's life history represents an extreme within the Cheloniidae family, prioritizing longevity and delayed reproduction for the sake of high lifetime fecundity. The measured lifespan of 80 years [am = 80 years] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] far exceeds that of smaller sea turtle species, such as the olive ridley, which seldom surpasses 50 years. Furthermore, the ultimate curved carapace length of 143 centimeters [Li = 143 centimeters] recorded from the literature stands as a global benchmark, demonstrating the species' capacity for exceptional somatic growth under favorable oceanic conditions. Conversely, the critical threshold for first reproduction at 29 years after birth [tR = 29 years after birth] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] imposes a long generation time that makes the population particularly sensitive to increased juvenile mortality from anthropogenic threats such as bycatch and habitat degradation. The relationship between these life-history parameters—particularly the interplay between the 91-centimeter (91 centimeters) [Lp = 91 centimeters] carapace length at puberty and the 130,000-gram (130,000 grams) [Wwi = 130,000 grams] ultimate adult weight—provides a framework for evaluating the health of the Ningaloo aggregation and for modeling the population's resilience to environmental change.
